intro: Forty five verses of history turned into a hymn. It opens with ten plural imperatives, give thanks, call, make known, sing, seek, remember, then drops the commands and runs the rest of the story on the narrative tense, one vav-consecutive verb after another. That is the most common verb form in biblical prose, and this is a good place to learn it because the sentences are short and the vocabulary repeats. Verses 1 to 15 appear almost word for word in 1 Chronicles 16, in the account of the ark coming up to Jerusalem, and the Hodu passage of the morning service is taken from that version. Notice what the psalm leaves out: from Abraham to the land, not one Israelite sin. Psalm 106, its neighbour, tells the same history with almost nothing else.

stichs.en: Give thanks to the LORD, call on His name;
make His deeds known among the peoples.

verses.summary: Three plural imperatives in seven words: give thanks, call, make known. The last one points outward, to the nations, before the story of Israel has begun.

stichs.en: Sing to Him, sing praise to Him;
speak of all His wonders.

verses.summary: Two verbs for singing, then a third that means to talk something over. Praise here includes conversation about what happened, not only music.

stichs.en: Glory in His holy name;
let the heart of those who seek the LORD rejoice.

verses.summary: The only boasting the psalm allows is boasting in a name that is not yours. In the second line the subject is the heart, not the person.

stichs.en: Seek the LORD and His strength;
seek His face always.

verses.summary: Seek twice, with two different verbs. The object shifts from the LORD and His strength to His face, which in the psalms means presence rather than a body.

stichs.en: Remember the wonders He has done,
His portents and the judgments of His mouth,

verses.summary: The call to praise ends with a call to remember, and remembering is the hinge. The next forty verses are the content of that memory.

stichs.en: you seed of Abraham His servant,
you sons of Jacob, His chosen ones.

verses.summary: The audience is named at last, and named by descent. Two construct chains, seed of and sons of, place the singers inside the story about to be told.

stichs.en: He is the LORD our God;
His judgments are in all the earth.

verses.summary: One clause of theology before the narrative starts. The jurisdiction claimed is global, which matters for a story about a single family.

stichs.en: He remembers His covenant forever,
the word He commanded to a thousand generations,

verses.summary: The verb remembered now governs the rest of the psalm. God is the one doing the remembering here, not the congregation that was told to remember in verse 5.

stichs.en: which He cut with Abraham,
and His oath to Isaac,

verses.summary: The idiom for making a covenant is cutting one, from the halved animals of the ceremony in Genesis 15. The oath to Isaac is the same promise reissued.

stichs.en: and He set it up for Jacob as a statute,
for Israel as an everlasting covenant,

verses.summary: One promise, three recipients, three legal words: statute, covenant, eternity. The repetition is not decoration, it is how a title deed gets drafted.

stichs.en: saying: To you I give the land of Canaan,
the portion of your inheritance.

verses.summary: The content of the covenant, quoted as direct speech, is a piece of real estate. The word for portion is a measuring rope, the surveyor's tool.

stichs.en: when they were men few in number,
very few, and strangers in it,

verses.summary: The promise comes first and the facts come second: the heirs are a handful of resident aliens who own none of the land. That gap is the psalm's subject.

stichs.en: and they went about from nation to nation,
from one kingdom to another people,

verses.summary: Movement with no arrival. The syntax repeats from and to twice, which is what having no country sounds like in Hebrew.

stichs.en: He let no one oppress them,
and He rebuked kings on their account:

verses.summary: Protection is described as restraint placed on other people. The kings are rebuked rather than destroyed, and the family never has to fight.

stichs.en: Do not touch My anointed ones,
and do My prophets no harm.

verses.summary: The only divine speech in the psalm besides the land grant, and both halves of it are negative commands. The covenant is enforced by what outsiders are forbidden to do.

stichs.en: And He called a famine upon the land;
He broke every staff of bread.

verses.summary: The famine is summoned like a servant. Staff of bread is an idiom for the supply that holds a household upright, so breaking it means removing support.

stichs.en: He sent a man before them;
as a slave Joseph was sold.

verses.summary: The sentence hides the brothers. Someone sent, someone was sold, and only at the end of the line does the name Joseph appear.

stichs.en: They bruised his foot with the fetter;
iron came upon his soul.

verses.summary: Two body parts under metal in two clauses, foot and soul. The second clause reverses the expected direction: the iron comes to him, not he to the iron.

stichs.en: until the time his word came to pass,
the saying of the LORD refined him.

verses.summary: Time is measured by a word arriving, and two different nouns for word sit in one verse. The prison is described as an assay, the test that separates metal from dross.

stichs.en: The king sent and released him,
the ruler of peoples, and set him free.

verses.summary: The king is the subject of three verbs and is never named. Release is said twice, once as untying and once as opening.

stichs.en: He made him lord over his house,
and ruler over all his property,

verses.summary: The prisoner of verse 18 now holds authority over a house and its holdings. The reversal is told in six words with no comment attached.

stichs.en: to bind his princes at his will,
and to teach his elders wisdom.

verses.summary: Binding returns, but Joseph is doing it now, and to princes. The last verb is teaching, which is what this whole section is being used to illustrate.

stichs.en: And Israel came to Egypt,
and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham.

verses.summary: One man's two names carry a whole nation into a new country. Ham is the ancestor of Egypt in the table of nations, so the geography here is genealogical.

stichs.en: And He made His people very fruitful,
and made them stronger than their foes.

verses.summary: The growth fulfils the promise made to the fathers and triggers everything that follows. Strength here is comparative, measured against the people next door.

stichs.en: He turned their heart to hate His people,
to deal craftily with His servants.

verses.summary: The turning of the heart is attributed to God, the same difficulty the Exodus narrative raises about Pharaoh. The psalm states it without softening it.

stichs.en: He sent Moses His servant,
Aaron, whom He had chosen.

verses.summary: Two names, one sent and one chosen. Against the massed adversaries of the preceding verses stand exactly two men.

stichs.en: They set among them the words of His signs,
and portents in the land of Ham.

verses.summary: An unusual construct, the words of His signs, treats the plagues as speech. The signs are placed among the Egyptians rather than merely done to them.

stichs.en: He sent darkness and it grew dark,
and they did not rebel against His word.

verses.summary: Darkness comes first here, though it is ninth in Exodus. The second line is the most argued sentence in the psalm, and the remez note below sets out why.

stichs.en: He turned their waters into blood,
and killed their fish.

verses.summary: Water into blood, then the death of what lives in the water. Cause and consequence are packed into a single verse with the same verb pattern twice.

stichs.en: Their land swarmed with frogs,
in the chambers of their kings.

verses.summary: The verb for swarming is the one used of small creatures on the fifth day of Genesis 1, so creation is running in the wrong direction. The frogs reach the royal bedrooms.

stichs.en: He spoke, and a swarm of flies came,
gnats in all their territory.

verses.summary: He spoke and it came, the shape of the creation account used destructively. Two species share one verse, which keeps the list moving fast.

stichs.en: He gave them hail for their rain,
flaming fire in their land.

verses.summary: Hail is given in place of rain, so the language of gift is kept and inverted. Fire and ice occupy the same sky in the same sentence.

stichs.en: And He struck their vine and their fig tree,
and shattered the trees of their territory.

verses.summary: Vine and fig tree are the standard biblical pair for settled prosperity. Striking them is striking the idea of a country secure enough to plant slow crops.

stichs.en: He spoke, and the locust came, and the hopper,
beyond number,

verses.summary: The opening of verse 31 repeats word for word, which is how a list builds pressure. What arrives this time cannot be counted at all.

stichs.en: and it ate every plant in their land,
and it ate the fruit of their ground.

verses.summary: The same verb twice, ate and ate, first the green growth and then the fruit. Nothing is left at either stage of the season.

stichs.en: And He struck every firstborn in their land,
the first of all their vigour.

verses.summary: The last plague is told with no dialogue and no Passover. First of their vigour is a biblical idiom for the eldest son as his father's first strength.

stichs.en: And He brought them out with silver and gold,
and none among His tribes stumbled.

verses.summary: Leaving with property answers what was said to Abraham in Genesis 15 about his descendants coming out with great possessions. Nobody stumbles, which prepares the desert march.

stichs.en: Egypt rejoiced when they went out,
for dread of them had fallen upon them.

verses.summary: Egypt is glad to see them go, and the reason given is fear. The gladness is relief, not goodwill, and the psalm says so in the same breath.

stichs.en: He spread a cloud as a screen,
and fire to give light at night.

verses.summary: Cloud and fire, the two forms of the wilderness escort. Each gets a stated function here: shade during the day, light after dark.

stichs.en: He asked, and He brought quail,
and satisfied them with the bread of heaven.

verses.summary: The first verb is singular though the sense needs the whole people, and translators have handled that differently for two thousand years. Quail and manna are compressed into one line.

stichs.en: He opened a rock and waters flowed;
they ran through the dry places, a river.

verses.summary: Water out of rock, and then a verb of walking applied to it. The desert is given a stream that behaves like a traveller crossing it.

stichs.en: For He remembered His holy word
with Abraham His servant.

verses.summary: The reason clause, held back until now. Everything from the famine onward happened because of a sentence spoken to one man centuries before any of it.

stichs.en: And He brought His people out with gladness,
His chosen ones with a glad cry.

verses.summary: Two different words for joy in one line, one interior and one audible. The exit is staged as a procession rather than an escape.

stichs.en: And He gave them the lands of nations,
and they inherited the labour of peoples,

verses.summary: The land arrives, and with it the work other people already put into it. The psalm names that cost plainly instead of leaving it out.

stichs.en: so that they would keep His statutes and guard His teachings.
Halleluyah.

verses.summary: The purpose of the whole history fits in one subordinate clause, and the purpose is keeping. The final word is the short form of the Name.

pardes.body: Seven blocks. A call to praise (1 to 6), the covenant sworn to the fathers (7 to 11), the protection of a handful of migrants (12 to 15), Joseph (16 to 22), Egypt and the plagues (23 to 36), the exit and the desert (37 to 41), and the reason for all of it (42 to 45). One verb frames the narrative: {{8.0}} where it begins and {{42.1}} where it ends, both meaning He remembered. The plague list is a selection, not a chronicle. Eight appear rather than ten, with no cattle plague and no boils, and darkness is moved from ninth place to first. The psalm also runs out of story before Sinai: the sequence goes promise, danger, deliverance, land, and never passes through a mountain.

The hardest line in the psalm is {{28.3}} {{28.4}}, and they did not rebel against His word. Who is not rebelling? Taken of the Egyptians it is odd, since resistance is the whole plot. Taken of Moses and Aaron it follows verse 27 well. The Greek version lacks the negative and reads that they rebelled, and modern translations still divide over which text to follow, so this is genuinely disputed rather than settled. Two smaller oddities reward attention. {{40.0}} is a singular verb, he asked, where the sense wants the people, and the old versions quietly make it plural. And {{11.6}}, rendered portion, is literally a measured rope: the surveyor's line became the ordinary word for an allotment of land.

Verse 15 is the psalm's only divine speech apart from the land grant, and it gives the patriarchs two titles, anointed and prophets. The second has a hook in the text: in Genesis 20 God tells Abimelech that Abraham is a prophet who will pray for him. Read this way the psalm functions as a charter. The claim to the land rests on an oath sworn to three individuals who owned nothing at the time, which is why the fathers are named and the generation at Sinai is not mentioned at all. The Joseph section carries the same logic on a small scale: the man thrown into a pit ends up holding the granary that keeps his family alive, so the descent gets read as provision arranged in advance rather than as an accident survived.

Remembering, in this psalm, is not a state of mind but an act that changes the world, and the two occurrences of the verb hold the whole narrative between them like brackets. The mystical reading takes the small numbers seriously: {{12.1}} {{12.2}}, men of number, few enough to be counted, is the narrow point through which the entire promise has to pass, and the smallness is a condition of the thing rather than an obstacle to it. Joseph goes down first so that what comes after can be gathered up, the pattern later kabbalah generalises as descent for the sake of ascent. The psalm then ends on {{45.5}} {{45.6}}, the shortest praise built on the shortest form of the Name, as though four hundred years of history compressed back down into two syllables.
